facts.label: The facts of one incident, filled in by code (klaxon.agent.postmortem) from a gated run's saved evidence: its run.json, the gate's request, decision and log, and the loop's trace. Each fact says where it comes from. The incident: a fault injected on purpose into a payments system on one machine, with synthetic data and a simulated provider, so no real money.

run.title: Payments fail: the provider hangs, and our circuit breaker fails fast
run.what_it_was: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, provider-outage, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, offered one write action (rollback_deploy), which runs only if a person approves it at the gate, and stopped on diagnosed after 10 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.

timeline.what: The alert rules were quiet at 2 evaluations in a row, and the money check passed: the stack was ready for the fault.
The fault's injection began, on purpose (klaxon.faults): at the provider: charges and refunds held 5 s, then 503. It took 0 s.

The alert PaymentsErrorsHigh fired, raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed: Payments are failing: over the last minute, 92% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx (8.78 per second), above the threshold of 20%. Payments are slow: over the last minute, the p95 latency of POST /payments on payments-api was 4.3 s, above the threshold of 2 s.

Klaxon's loop began to investigate the alert: claude-opus-5-5 through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, with read-only tools, offered one write action (rollback_deploy) that runs only if a person approves it.
The loop stopped: diagnosed (confidence 0.65), after 10 steps and 8 tool calls, in 50.5 s.
The diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one.
The harness's clearing, its safety net, asked for the provider answering again. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.
The rules read the stack again after the clearing: no alert fired; the money check passed.

model_words.note: the loop's own words, from a model: data, not checked by code
model_words.hypothesis: At about 03:13:30 the provider (fake-provider, external) degraded. Some POST /v1/payments calls hung until our 3 s read timeout and a few returned 500. payments-api retries each call, so one request took 9.6 s (3 attempts of 3 s each), which pushed p95 above 2 s. The failures opened payments-api's circuit breaker. Since 03:13:56 most POST /payments requests fail fast with 503 and the payment is left pending, which gives the 92% 5xx rate. No change on our side lines up with the onset: every container was created together at 03:12:03. The breaker is shedding load as designed; it is not the cause. Open: the client metrics (c4, c5) seem not to record timeouts, so I cannot count them. I saw no provider-side data. The money check was not run, so payments the provider charged after we timed out are unverified.
model_words.fix_summary: No rollback is needed. Escalate the timeouts and 500s on /v1/payments to the provider, and keep the breaker on. After the provider recovers, run the money check and reconcile the pending payments, including timed-out calls the provider may have charged. Follow-up: record timeouts in the client-duration and provider-attempts metrics.
model_words.blast_radius: None of our services changes. Payments keep returning 503 and staying pending until the provider recovers. The provider may have charged some timed-out payments while our caller got no 201. Webhooks and the money check should resolve them.
model_words.rollback_plan: Nothing to undo: this proposes no action. If the provider turns out to be healthy, reopen the investigation into payments-api's network path and its timeout settings.

narrative.summary: On 2026-11-01, a fault called provider-outage was injected on purpose into a payments system on one machine. The system ran with synthetic data and a simulated provider, so no real money moved. The provider's charge and refund API hung and then answered 503. The alert PaymentsErrorsHigh fired 47 s after the fault. Klaxon's loop investigated and stopped on diagnosed with confidence 0.65. A grading rule found that its diagnosis named the recorded cause. The diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one, and no action ran. The harness's clearing removed the fault's cause. After the clearing, no alert fired and the money check passed. 299 payments and 9 refunds were still pending at the client's last status check.
narrative.timeline: At 03:13:35 UTC the alert rules were quiet at 2 evaluations in a row, and the money check passed, so the stack was ready. The fault's injection then began at the provider, and it took 0 s. The facts give no clock time for it. At 03:14:23 UTC, 47 s after the fault, the alert PaymentsErrorsHigh fired. At 03:14:24 UTC, 48 s after the fault, Klaxon's loop began to investigate. It ran claude-opus-5-5 through Claude Code on Aravind's seat. It had tools that could only read, and it was offered one write action, rollback_deploy, gated on a person's approval. At 03:15:14 UTC, 98.5 s after the fault, the loop stopped on diagnosed after 10 steps and 8 tool calls, in 50.5 s. The diagnosis named no action. At 98.5 s after the fault, the harness's clearing asked for the provider to answer again. At 03:16:44 UTC, 188.5 s after the fault, the rules read the stack again. No alert fired, and the money check passed.
narrative.impact: The alert said that over the last minute, 92% of the answers to POST /payments on payments-api were 5xx, at 8.78 per second, above the threshold of 20%. It also said the p95 latency of POST /payments was 4.3 s, above the threshold of 2 s. The money check passed at the alert, with a lag of 0 for the ledger and 0 for payment-confirmer. It passed again at 03:16:44 UTC, after the clearing. The synthetic clients sent 3 new payments per second, on average. 810 payments arrived, and 810 got an answer. 511 succeeded, 0 were refused, and 0 got an answer the clients did not expect. 299 were left with their outcome unknown, and all 299 were still pending at the client's last status check. For refunds, 50 succeeded, 0 were refused, and 9 were left with their outcome unknown. All 9 were still pending at the last status check. The clients retried 974 times, and 0 requests were shed. The evidence does not say whether the pending payments and refunds settled since. These were synthetic clients, not real customers.
narrative.cause: The recorded cause was that the provider's charge and refund API hung for 5 s and then answered 503. Our payments API's calls to it timed out, each after 3 attempts. Its circuit breaker opened after 5 calls in a row got no answer. From then on the API failed fast. It answered 503 with outcome unknown at once, without calling the provider. It let one trial call through 10 s after it opened, and again after each trial that failed. The errors and slow answers raised the alert. Klaxon's diagnosis said the provider degraded, calls hung and timed out, retries pushed latency up, and the breaker opened and made most requests fail fast. It said the breaker was shedding load as designed and was not the cause. A rule in klaxon.grading, rubric version 3, found that it named every required element: the provider, the hang, and the open breaker. The rule reads words, not meaning. Some details in the diagnosis did not match the recorded cause. It described a different timeout length, and some error answers other than 503. It also said the money check was not run, but the facts show the money check passed at the alert.
narrative.response: Klaxon was offered one write action, rollback_deploy, which would run only if a person approved it at the gate. Its diagnosis named no action and judged that no rollback was needed. Since no action was named, nobody was asked to approve one, and nothing ran. Nothing was verified, because no action ran. The diagnosis proposed to escalate to the provider, keep the breaker on, and reconcile the pending payments after recovery. Those words are the model's own and were not checked by code. The fault's cause was not a deploy. It was removed by the harness's clearing, its safety net, at 98.5 s after the fault. After the clearing, the rules saw no alert and the money check passed.
narrative.repairs: The last money check passed at 03:16:44 UTC, after the clearing, so nothing in the books is left to repair. Up to its cutoff, the provider held no charge or refund that our records did not show as succeeded. So any payment or refund still pending had no money moved for it. 299 payments and 9 refunds were still pending at the client's last status check. Each one still pending needs a decision, either a retry with its key or marking it failed. A refund left pending blocks new refunds on its payment until it settles. The recorded remedy says nothing needs to change on our side, and that the provider must recover, with an escalation to it. The evidence does not name who must make these decisions, so a person reviewing this incident must assign them. The diagnosis also suggested recording timeouts in the client duration and provider attempts metrics. That suggestion is the model's own and was not checked.
